A2.text:
Elvin is twenty-six and lives alone. He thinks he is very handy. “I can repair anything,” he always says.

One night, at midnight, he heard a sound in the kitchen: drip, drip, drip. There was a leak under the sink.

Elvin did not want to call anyone. He found some tape and put it around the pipe. “A temporary fix,” he said, and went to bed.

In the morning, the floor was wet. Elvin watched a video and took his tools. He wanted to be fast, so he decided to cut corners. He did not turn off the water first. When he opened the pipe, water came out everywhere!

Elvin called his grandfather, Ramiz. Ramiz is seventy, but he can fix cars, chairs, lamps and phones. He is a jack of all trades.

Ramiz came in thirty minutes with a big box. First, he turned off the water. Then he looked at the pipe. “This rubber ring is worn out,” he said. He took a spare part from his box and changed it. In ten minutes, the leak stopped.

Then Ramiz saw a chair. “Why is this chair in pieces?” he asked.

“It was a little loose,” Elvin said. “I wanted to fix it.”

Ramiz laughed. “Was it really broken? Remember: if it ain't broke, don't fix it.”

B1.text:
Elvin considered himself extremely handy. He owned a drill he had used twice, a set of screwdrivers still in their plastic case and an unshakeable belief that any repair could be learned from a ten-minute video.

At midnight on Tuesday, he heard it: a slow drip coming from under the kitchen sink. He opened the cupboard and found a small but steady leak where two pipes met. Calling a plumber at that hour was out of the question, so he wrapped half a roll of tape around the joint. “Temporary fix,” he told himself proudly, and went back to bed.

By morning, the tape had given up and there was a lake under the sink. Elvin found a video, lined up his tools and decided to cut corners: turning off the main water supply meant finding the valve behind the washing machine, and that seemed like too much effort. He unscrewed the joint. Water shot out like a fountain, straight into his face.

Ten minutes later, standing in two centimetres of water, he phoned his grandfather.

Ramiz was seventy-two and a true jack of all trades. He had repaired tractors in his village, radios in the eighties and, more recently, the screens of half his neighbours' phones. He arrived in thirty minutes with a metal toolbox older than Elvin.

He turned off the water without comment, unscrewed the joint and held up a small black ring. “Worn out,” he said. “Twenty years old, probably.” He found a spare part in his box, fitted it and tightened everything. The leak stopped completely.

Then he noticed the kitchen chair lying in pieces by the window. “What happened here?”

“One leg was a bit loose,” Elvin admitted. “I thought I'd fix it while I had the tools out.”

Ramiz picked up a screw and sighed. “Grandson, listen to an old man. If it ain't broke, don't fix it. And next time, call me before the flood, not after.”

B2.text:
Elvin regarded himself as exceptionally handy, a reputation based almost entirely on his own testimony. His equipment consisted of a cordless drill used precisely twice, a screwdriver set still sealed in its plastic case and an unwavering conviction that no repair on earth required more than a ten-minute tutorial.

The trouble began at midnight on Tuesday with a faint, rhythmic drip beneath the kitchen sink. Torch in hand, he traced it to a modest leak at the joint between two pipes. Ringing a plumber at that hour was unthinkable, so he wound half a roll of electrical tape around the joint, admired his handiwork and returned to bed, satisfied that his temporary fix would hold until the weekend.

It held until approximately four in the morning. By the time his alarm went off, a shallow lake had formed beneath the sink. Elvin selected a video, arranged his tools on a towel like a surgeon and resolved to cut corners: shutting off the main supply would mean dragging out the washing machine to reach the valve, and the video, after all, made the whole thing look trivial. He loosened the joint. A jet of water hit him squarely in the face.

Standing in two centimetres of water, he swallowed his pride and phoned his grandfather.

Ramiz was seventy-two and a jack of all trades in the oldest sense: he had kept Soviet tractors running in his village, mended radios through the eighties and, in his retirement, become the unofficial repair service for every cracked phone screen in his building. He arrived within half an hour carrying a dented metal toolbox considerably older than his grandson.

Without a word of reproach, he moved the washing machine, shut off the water and dismantled the joint. He held up a small, perished black ring. “Worn out,” he said. “Probably original to the building.” He produced the right spare part from a jar of assorted washers, fitted it and tightened the joint. The leak stopped completely.

Only then did he notice the kitchen chair lying in pieces beneath the window.

“One leg was slightly loose,” Elvin explained, avoiding his eye. “Since the tools were out anyway…”

Ramiz turned a stray screw over in his fingers and sighed the sigh of three generations. “If it ain't broke, don't fix it,” he said. “And, my dear boy — next time, ring me before the flood.”

podcast.title: A tap with tape on it

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Can you fix things at home? Guess: what is wrong in Sam's kitchen?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is fixing things. Leyla, are you handy at home?
Not really. When something breaks, I call my neighbour, Mr Aliyev. He can repair anything.
Lucky you. I need someone like that.
[laugh] He has more tools than a shop.
Well, I need him. My kitchen tap has a leak. Drip, drip, drip, all night.
Oh no. What did you do?
I put tape around it. A temporary fix. That was three months ago.
[chuckle] Three months is not temporary, Sam!
I know. The real problem is a spare part. The shop says it comes from Germany.
My grandmother never throws anything away. Her old radio is fifty years old, and it still works.
How?
My grandad repaired it again and again. When a button was loose, he fixed it with a tiny screw.
Things lasted longer back then. Now a phone feels old after three years.
That's true. Do you repair your own things?
Only my running shoes. They're completely worn out, but I glued the sole back on.
Sam! Your half marathon is soon. Don't cut corners with your shoes.
You're right. A cheap repair could cost me a broken ankle.
So — new shoes this week?
New shoes. And maybe I'll finally call Mr Aliyev about the tap.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what was the last thing you fixed yourself — and how did it go?
Mine is a tap with tape on it. See you next time!
Bye for now!
